answer.summary:
You come across as an organiser with a warm centre. High conscientiousness, high agreeableness, and moderate extraversion in a way that surprises people who assume you are an extrovert because you are always at the thing. You post in clusters around events you arranged, then go quiet for a fortnight. That is not inconsistency; it is recovery.

What you value shows up in what you do rather than what you say. Four years of captions and barely a sentence about yourself that is not attached to somebody else's news. Generous with attention, sparing with disclosure — which reads as modesty and works as a wall.

At work the same shape holds. You notice what has not been assigned and do it, which makes you indispensable and, on this evidence, slightly under-credited.

strengths.detail: Dates, follow-ups, the thing someone was nervous about last month. Your comments return to other people's earlier posts with a specificity that is hard to fake and rare to find.

career.watchOuts: Somewhere with no natural end to the work, or a culture where credit goes to whoever claims it loudest.

bonus.harsh:
You have saved about 140 recipes and training plans over four years, and your own captions show the same three trailheads and the same twelve-week block on repeat every one of those years. That folder is not a plan, it is a shrine. Meanwhile the actual pattern here is beautifully consistent: you do things for people without being asked, and you have never once, in four years of posts, asked anyone for anything back. That is not generosity running unchecked, it is a ledger you have decided not to show anyone — which is why 'quietly tallying' shows up in your own relationship read a page ago, and why nobody around you has learned to reciprocate, because you have never given them the information required to try.

And the tell is the thing that is not here at all: forty-one posts closing out a plan, zero admitting the plan was heavy. An organiser who never once says the load is a lot is not calm, they are unwilling to find out what happens if they put it down for a week and see who notices.
bonus.advice: Cook one of the hundred and forty recipes instead of saving a hundred and forty-first — the gap between the folder and the plate is the actual finding, not the folder. Unfollow the five hundred and ninety-three accounts you have not engaged with in a year; a subscription you are not reading is not community, it is guilt with a notification badge. And say the specific thing out loud to one specific person: not 'I'm fine', the actual sentence — 'I need you to plan the next one' or 'I noticed you didn't ask how my week was' — because a need that is never stated is a need nobody can meet, and you already know that, you just have not tried saying it where it could be heard.

premiumAnalysis.regret:
If the quiet-organiser pattern holds, the regret most likely to find you is not a missed chance but a missing person: you. Four years of posts plan trips, birthdays and deadlines for everyone else, and 41 of 47 deadlines were closed, yet no caption in all that time says what you wanted, or that the load was heavy.

People who live this way rarely regret the help they gave. They regret that nobody, themselves included, ever got to know what they would have chosen. One thing to do this month: plan one day around something only you want, put it in the calendar before anyone else's plans, and tell one person about it afterwards.

receiving.why: The posts you write most warmly about are unhurried and undivided — a long walk, a slow dinner, nowhere to be afterwards.

receiving.line: Specific beats effusive — name the thing you noticed.
receiving.why: The rare posts where you quote something someone said about you are kept and repeated.

giving.line: You show love by removing a problem, often before it is mentioned.
giving.why: Your account is a four-year record of doing things for people: the lifts, the bookings, the collecting, the cooking.

loveLanguages.caveat: Love languages are a popular framework rather than a validated instrument. Read these as a decent guess at what you reach for, not a diagnosis.

bring.title: You remember
bring.detail: Dates, follow-ups, the thing someone was nervous about last month. Your comments return to other people's earlier posts with a specificity that is hard to fake and rare to find.

bring.title: Low-drama by default
bring.detail: Four years without a single public disagreement is not avoidance on this evidence — it reads as someone who handles friction privately and promptly.

hard.title: You do not ask
hard.detail: There is almost no example here of you requesting anything for yourself. In a close relationship that becomes a problem for the other person, who is left guessing and eventually gets it wrong.

hard.title: Score-keeping in silence
hard.detail: The same giving-first pattern: generous in the moment, quietly tallying, and inclined to feel unmet without ever having stated the need. Nothing here shows it blowing up, but the ingredients are visible.

others.title: Finishes things
others.detail: The follow-through rate visible in this account is the trait most organisations are shortest of. You close what you open.

others.title: Holds the group together
others.detail: You reliably do the unassigned work that keeps a team functioning — the scheduling, the chasing, the remembering.

holding.title: Under-claims
holding.detail: You narrate collective wins and almost never individual ones. On this evidence you are more likely to be under-credited than over-credited, and unlikely to correct it.

holding.title: Absorbs the overflow
holding.detail: Work that has no owner appears to become yours by default. That is why you are valuable and why you are probably tired.

howYouWork.workStyle: Plans in blocks, announces the plan, delivers to it. High standards applied quietly rather than argued for.
howYouWork.watchOuts: Somewhere with no natural end to the work, or a culture where credit goes to whoever claims it loudest.

build.title: Your follow-through
build.detail: You close what you open, which most people and most teams are short of. Use it deliberately: pick the commitments you take on rather than inheriting them.

build.title: The circle you keep
build.detail: The same close group for years is rare and worth protecting. It is also where you could start being looked after as well as looking after.

develop.title: Let the credit land
develop.detail: You narrate collective wins and almost never your own part in them, so the people who rely on you most may not know how much you carry. Under pressure your reliability tips into absorbing everyone's overflow.

method.rationale: Four years of steady, well-dated posting, and captions long enough to read tone from rather than guess at — that is about as much as an export gives. Beliefs and attachment are the thinner end: you write warmly but rarely about yourself, so those two lean on indirect evidence while everything above them rests on behaviour that repeats.

card.why: Like her, you step up for the people around you and see it through: four years of posts naming a plan and closing it out. When it goes well, the win is written as ours rather than mine, the same quiet competence that shares the credit.
